pr_comments: As discussion in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/21633 has ramped up I wanted to get this draft PR open for direct feedback. @martinschmatz put together a POC a while back based on his proposal, I took the POC patch and cleaned it up. It still has work to be done, but we wanted to handle further clean up in parallel with community feedback. @martinschmatz provided detailed documentation with his POC that I will share here once I update all the markdown links pointing to different code sections

The following is part of the documentation provided by @martinschmatz with his original patch

## Implementation remarks

Variables to keep track of key shares are added [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L1315) for temporary use during session establishment, [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L1618) to extensions for a session, and [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L1023) for the context. We limit clients to send a maximum of `OPENSSL_CLIENT_MAX_KEY_SHARES` (which is [defined](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L790) to be 4) and tested not to be exceeded [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L672).  

The 'heavy lifting' is done in two parts: First during the parsing of the list of groups, and then during an actual session establishment. 

__List parsing__

The list of groups are processed via [SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list](https://www.openssl.org/docs/manmaster/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list.html) which uses [SSL_CTX_ctrl](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_lib.c#L3073) procedure for SSL processing, where [tls1_set_groups_list](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_lib.c#L3079) is called with all `NULL` parameters, and [ssl3_ctx_ctrl](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/s3_lib.c#L3881) for TLS also calls [tls1_set_groups_list](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/s3_lib.c#L3718) but with valid parameters.

To accommodate key shares, the [definition](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L2808) and [implementation](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1148) of `tls1_set_groups_list` is extended to enable passing variable locations for the code points of a key share (via `ksext`), the number of key shares (via `ksextlen`) plus an indicator that '!' prefix(es) were identified (via `ks_selection_detected`).

As a helper, a function [tls1_get_requested_keyshare_groups](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L846) is added (including [declaration](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L2824)) which provides the pointers to the key share variables (array and length of array).

The function [tls1_set_groups_list](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1148) (with declaration [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_local.h#L2824)) is used to parse the string with the list of groups (`const char *str`). It is using a call-back function [gid_cb](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1060) provided to `CONF_parse_list` which does the actual processing. `CONF_parse_list` uses the call-back function for each group iteratively (read: the call-back function processes one group at the time). The call-back function gets a struct [gid_cb_st](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1050) as parameter in which variables for key shares were [added](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1055). The presence of '!'-prefixes is checked first in the callback function and kept track via `add_keyshare` flag. After some [memory allocation](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1111), the key-share info is added [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1139) if needed (= whenever a '!' prefix was detected), which is eventually fed back [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1195). For backward compatibility, preparation for generating a keyshare for the first group in the list in case no '!' was present in the entire list is done [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1183).

__Session establishment__

As a first step, the info from the context is [copied](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_lib.c#L846) over to the session.

The `ClientHello` packet for key shares is constructed using [tls_construct_ctos_key_share](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L692). A [check](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L713) is done to find out whether the built-in default list is being used, for which the list of supported groups is used, or whether the list of requested key shares can be used. Then, three scenarios are processed: 

- The situation where a `HelloRetryRequest` must be [processed](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L727), 
- where the [default, built-in list](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L734) is being used, and 
- where the [list of requested key shares](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L759) can be applied. 
 
In all cases, the key share extension network packet is added using a helper function [add_key_share](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L629) which was extended to keep track about how often it was called (to add a key share for the first group in the list, which is also instrumental for the case of using the default, built-in list). It is [checked](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L672) that not to many keyshares are sent.
It then finally keeps track of the key shares to be added [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L677) with initialization of how many keyshares were added [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_clnt.c#L725).

## Server Side

For the server side, a new group selection algorithm was implemented. It is only used if there's at least one '!' prefix in the list of server-side supported groups, the 'old' algorithm is used otherwise. 

For the server side group selection algorithm, 4 possibilities exist, with sequence is priority (=> read table below like so: If entries in the client side list have overlap with the the server side list, do the overlap action; if not, use the next line and repeat):
```
   Client                  Server                    If they overlap
1) keyshare list           requested keyshare list   Use leftmost group_id from server requested keyshare list
2) supported groups list   requested keyshare list   HRR with leftmost group_id from server requested keyshare list
3) keyshare list           supported groups list     Use leftmost group_id from server groups list
4) supported groups list   supported groups list     HRR with leftmost group_id from server groups list
```
Therefore, for example, if a client sends a keyshare for a legacy group, but would also support a Q-safe 'group', the server would trigger a HRR for the Q-safe 'group' (and with that a round-trip) even if it would support the legacy group.

The 'heavy lifting' is again done in two parts: First during the parsing of the list of groups, and then during an actual session establishment. 

__List parsing__

Same code is used as for client side list parsing. 

__Session establishment__

As a first step, the info from the context is [copied](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/ssl_lib.c#L846) over to the session.

Most of the functionality is implemented during (a) the [parsing](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L605) of the `ClientHello`, and (b) the [construction](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1363) of the server keyshare.

When parsing the `ClientHello` in [tls_parse_ctos_key_share](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L605), we first [check](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L656) whther any '!' prefix was used. If not, we use exisitng code, but use [new code](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L725) othewise.

In the new code, we first [extract](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L730) all client shares from the `ClientHello` packet and we [get](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L745) the list of server groups which had a '!' prefix. In combination with the list of [supported groups for server and client](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L630), we have all the 4 lists we need to apply the new group selection algorithm. 

There's one caveat: While preparation of `ServerHello` (SH) is done in `tls_parse_ctos_key_share`, the `HelloRetryRequests` (HRR) are prepared later in `final_key_share`. But our algorithm requires a HRR in step 2 already followed by a SH in step 3 if step 2 was not successful. To solve this minor challenge, we [prepare](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L796) step 2 in `tls_parse_ctos_key_share` (using temporary variable `s3_tmp_group_id_supported_by_client`) which is then [applied](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1507) in `final_key_share`.

Other than the above caveat, all 4 scenarios are sequentially checked (and jumping over the remaining checks if one scenario applies) by simply scaning one list over the other ([1](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L771) , [prep2](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L796) & [2](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1502), [3](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L827), [4](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1513)).

We use one new helper function `check_in_list_pos` (see [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/statem_lib.c#L2599) and [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/statem_local.h#L70)) which also supplies the position of where a group was found in a list as opposed to `check_in_list` which only provides found / not_found info. 

It is finally worth mentioning that as soon as `s->s3.group_id` is initialized with a group ID in `tls_parse_ctos_key_share`, a SH will automatically be triggered. HRRs are triggered in `final_key_share` by setting `s->hello_retry_request = SSL_HRR_PENDING` ([here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1508) and [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1548)).

## Proposed Documentation

```
If a group name in SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list() is preceded with 
the ! character, the way key shares are generated on the client 
side and how groups are selected on the server side is influenced
during a TLS v1.3 handshake process:

On the client side, a ! prefix for a group in the list of groups will 
add a key share for this group in the ClientHello. By default, a 
maximum of four ! prefixes (for up to 4 key_shares) is supported, 
which can be influenced during build time by defining 
OPENSSL_CLIENT_MAX_KEY_SHARES with a different value.

If no ! prefix is present anywhere in the entire list of groups on the 
client-side, a single keyshare is sent for the leftmost group in the 
client-side list of groups.

Any ! prefix on the server side results in 'server preference' selection 
of the group: Upon receiving the ClientHello, the server 
builds four lists, two each from the information received from 
the client and from its own partially prefixed list of supported 
groups: client supported_groups (C_SG), client provided keys_share 
groups (C_KS), all server supported_groups (S_SG), server ! prefixed 
groups (S_PG). It then stepwise evaluates these lists pairwise 
as per table below and takes the resulting action if an overlap 
is detected, or the server sends an Alert (21) "Fatal (2), Handshake 
failure (40)" if no overlap was detected in any of the steps:

     |  Client  Server | Server action   Using leftmost over- 
Step |  list    list   | if overlap      lapping group from 
-----------------------------------------------------------
 1   |  C_KS    S_PG   |     SH                S_PG
 2   |  C_SG    S_PG   |     HRR               S_PG
 3   |  C_KS    S_SG   |     SH                S_SG
 4   |  C_SG    S_SG   |     HRR               S_SG
[HRR = HelloRetryRequest, SH=ServerHello]

If no ! prefix is present anywhere in the entire list of groups on the 
server-side, 'client preference' principle is applied by the server to 
choose a group: The server will select the first key share group present 
in the ClientHello which it also supports. If no such key share is present, 
it will then select the first group in the list of supported_groups as 
received in the ClientHello which it also supports.

If no group list is explicitly specified (in code, in the OpenSSL or 
application config file, or on command line if supported by the 
application), the built-in list of groups is used, which implies 
that no ! prefix is specified.

The ! prefix can be used instead or in addition of the ? prefix
character. The sequence of the two letters in the latter case 
is irrelevant.
```

- Few TODOs (see [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L739) and [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/933e6b08a5a64caf1839d067cdca93da53a4df00/ssl/t1_lib.c#L1110)

My problem with this is still that a single (system-wide) configuration will not satisfy both server and client use cases.

E.g. with a (future) typical groups list (1) `X25519MLKEM768`, (2) `SecP256r1MLKEM768`, (3) `X25519`, (4) `P-256` :
* a client will want to prefix 1, 3 (and perhaps 4) to generate key_share for the most likely selected groups 
(i.e. not necessarily in most preferred order, but as a performance optimization)
* a server will want to prefix (at least) 1 and 2 to prefer PQ groups if at all possible (or everything, with PQ-first order).

So what should a generic default groups list look like?

This would be avoided if the server just selects a group based on the list order (disregarding prefix), i.e., treat the entire S_SG as S_PG in your table.

@ghen2 As @ajbozarth wrote, this is a first draft, based on state of knowledge some few months back. This with the intent that interested parties could start to play with it.

If the community agrees, I don't see any issue to jointly agree on a syntax for list of groups to cover (1) unified list, and (2) client or server preference on server-side. Need to think how an intuitive syntax would look like (after my vacation next two weeks).

@ghen2 I don't understand how this can address client or server preference on server-side. Do I miss something? 

I'm (preliminarily) thinking about something like `[ ( [ X ] [ Y ] ) ]` as syntax for a "zero-one-or-two-letters-in-brackets"-prefix, where:
- X controls the key-share to be added, suggested to have valid value of 'k',
- Y controls the preference on server side, suggested to have valid value of 'c' (client preference) or 's' (server preference),
- only either 'c' or 's' as prefix character allowed in entire list (in addition to 'k'),
- capital letters also allowed : (k) = (K), (Kc) = (kC)
- any sequence of letters allowed: (kS) = (sk) = (SK) =...
- no character inside '()' ignored.

The advantage of using '(' and ')' as prefix delimiters is that - in contrast to '!' - I'm not aware of any string operating app that would 'trigger' on those characters. 
I'm open to the suggestion that, in addition to the above, a '(p)' could be used in separated lists, triggering on client-side a key share to be sent (irrespective of 'p' or 'P'), and on server-side would mean client pref if small 'p', server pref if capital 'P'. This would be a replacement for the '!'-prefix in the draft implementation with added server-side preference selection. To be honest, I see unified list syntax as an outlier, to be supported of course, but not making it overly complicated for all the rest of us.

Using your example from further up, `(ks)X25519MLKEM768:(S)SecP256r1MLKEM768:(K)X25519:P-256` would be a valid unified group list where 
- the client sends key shares for `X25519MLKEM768` and `X25519` (in that order),
- the server selects the first available key share from groups `X25519MLKEM768` | `SecP256r1MLKEM768`, or then sends a HRR for the first of of these two that would be supported by the client, or then selects first key share from groups `X25519` | `P-256` if sent by the client, or then sends a HRR for the first of the groups `X25519` | `P-256` if one is supported by the client, or then lets the connection fail.

Separated for client and server, it would be
- for client `(p)X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768:(p)X25519:P-256`
- for server `(P)X25519MLKEM768:(P)SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519:P-256`

I liked the simplicity of individual marker characters better than partially-case-sensitive bracketted letter soup. :-)  
(And `?` already exists.)

Eg. `!` for key_share (client) and `*` for "worth a HRR" (server).  The same group would then look like:
`*!X25519MLKEM678:*SecP256r1MLKEM768:!X25519:P-256`

Or, to avoid introducing too many additional special characters that could confuse application config parsers, how about a `!` *prefix* for key_share, and `!` *suffix* for HRR worthy groups?
`!X25519MLKEM768!:SecP256r1MLKEM768!:!X25519:P-256`

> Eg. `!` for key_share (client) and `*` for "worth a HRR" (server). The same group would then look like:
> `*!X25519MLKEM678:*SecP256r1MLKEM768:!X25519:P-256

IMO instead of _worth a HRR_ marker you need HRR equivalency groups.
Let's imagine we want to prefer P-384 if there is no hybrid PQC available:

`(!X25519MLKEM678:SecP256r1MLKEM768):(P-384):(!X25519:P-256)` - i.e. HRR is caused if there is match in support in the first or the second equivalency group without a keyshare available. With your proposal, if P-384 was marked as worth HRR if there was a match both in hybrid set and P-384 but there was no keyshare for hybrid, there would be no HRR. And if P-384 was not marked as worth HRR and there would be match for it and X25519 and there was only X25519 key share, we would not get HRR either.

> how about a ! prefix for key_share, and ! suffix for HRR worthy groups

Hmmm....that sounds *really* confusing. Let's not go down that route.

> IMO instead of _worth a HRR_ marker you need HRR equivalency groups.
> Let's imagine we want to prefer P-384 if there is no hybrid PQC available:
> (!X25519MLKEM678:SecP256r1MLKEM768):(P-384):(!X25519:P-256)

I don't think supporting multiple layers of preference/equivalence as you suggest is really necessary.  The real-world use case would be to prefer PQC over non-PQC, and not, as in your example, P-384 over X25519 or P-256 (at least not at the cost of HRR).  Today openssl also considers all groups to have equivalent security.

And in that case, for the server-side, it would suffice to mark the "first _n_" groups as preferred, so a counter (_n_), or some end-of-list marker (like your brackets), instead of marking individual groups as preferred.  
Marking individual groups is only needed for client-side key_share preference, as these could be in different order.

Would a notation similar to `@SECLEVEL=n` be suitable for that?  So a combined client/server config could look like:

`!X25519MLKEM678:SecP256r1MLKEM768:!X25519:P-256:P-384:@HRR=2`

I do not see why the equivalency groups would be more complicated to implement than your proposal with `@HRR=2`.
It could save us having to add an additional mechanism in future if it is really needed for some use-cases.

Another one that I can imagine is _pure PQ_ groups vs _hybrid PQ_ groups with hybrid (at least initially before we get the confidence in PQ algos) being preferred but _pure PQ_ being preferred over non-PQ groups.
Hybrid PQ over pure PQ over traditional is indeed a plausible future use case for multi-tiered HRR preference, thanks for pointing out.

> 3.1) A means to specify two levels of priority for server side groups, e.g. level indication via pre-/post-fix, priority inside level either flat (client preference) or via left-to-right (server preference)

IMO limiting this to two levels is would be too restrictive for future use-cases.

A server vs. client side preference should IMO affect the selection only within the same priority level.

Imagine this configuration on the server side:
`(X25519MLKEM768:SecP256r1MLKEM768):(MLKEM768):(X25519:P-256)`
- we have 3 priority levels
- highest prio - hybrid KEMS, mid prio - pure PQ KEM, low prio - pure EC KEM

The server-side algorithm should be roughly:
1. filter out the groups not supported by the client, removing priority levels that have no match from the client's supported groups, keep this list
2. filter this list further to keep just the groups with key shares available from the configuration, but keep the existing priority levels
3. if there is no match in the highest priority group supported by both client and server (i.e. in the list from step 2) then select the first group from this priority group as indicated by client (on client preference) or as configured locally (on server preference) and send HRR
4. if there is a match in the highest priority group then select the first matching group as indicated by client (on client preference) or as configured locally (on server preference) 

Some examples against the server configuration above:
- client sends group list: `SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519MLKEM768:MLKEM768:X25519` key shares: `SecP256r1MLKEM768:P-256` - SecP256r1MLKEM768 is selected for handshake, no HRR needed
- client sends group list: `SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519MLKEM768:X25519` key shares: `SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519MLKEM768:X25519` - for client preference SecP256r1MLKEM768 is selected for handshake, for server preference X25519MLKEM768 is selected no HRR needed
- client sends group list: `SecP256r1MLKEM768:X25519MLKEM768:MLKEM768:X25519` key shares: `MLKEM768:X25519` - HRR is needed,  for client preference SecP256r1MLKEM768 is selected for HRR, for server preference X25519MLKEM768 is selected
- client sends group list: `MLKEM768:X25519:P-256` key shares: `X25519` - HRR is needed, MLKEM768 is selected for HRR
- client sends group list: `X25519:P-256` key shares: `P-256` - P-256 is selected for handshake, no HRR needed
In my proposal, the current configuration without any priority groups would be treated as a single priority group and that would keep the backwards compatibility with the existing stable releases.

issue_context.title: key_share / supported_group selection algorithm needs changes for post-quantum
issue_context.body:
OpenSSL's key_share / supported_group selection algorithm seems to be roughly:

1. Look for a match in the client key_share extension, picking the first, in client preference order, that the server supports. https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/91bc783a93a2a695fe6a2f8da93cf5b5e086ba42/ssl/statem/extensions_srvr.c#L634
2. If there was no match, pick the first group, in server preference order, that the client supports. https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/91bc783a93a2a695fe6a2f8da93cf5b5e086ba42/ssl/statem/extensions.c#L1446

This algorithm has some odd properties. First, it sometimes uses client preference order and sometimes server order, which is kind of weird. Also contrary to OpenSSL's [documentation](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.1/man3/SSL_set1_groups.html), which claims callers configure a preference order, yet it doesn't actually evaluate a coherent preference order on the server.

More importantly, it always prefer the non-HRR options over the HRR options, implicitly assuming that the client's choice of what to predict in key_share reflects its preferences. This assumption isn't supported by RFC 8446, and will likely to start breaking down with post-quantum, as the large keys will require clients to navigate tricky trade-offs. This mismatch means that OpenSSL servers may be downgraded to a classical algorithm in some cases, even when both sides support a post-quantum one.

For details, I wrote an Internet-Draft discussing the problem here:
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-davidben-tls-key-share-prediction/
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-davidben-tls-key-share-prediction-00.html
(For comments on the draft itself and overall problem, the TLSWG list at IETF is probably the best venue. I've filed this bug mostly in case you all don't follow that list. Also to make sure OpenSSL was aware that you all are indeed one of the TLS server implementations the draft refers to as having a problematic selection algorithm.)

Something like: (pqsig1,rsapsssha256),(ecdsa,eddsa) - first two subsets and second two subsets have no preference within but algos from the first subset are preferred against the second subset.

I think client order vs server order isn't that important, though being self-consistent is good. The root issue is whether you believe presence in `key_share` implies a strong preference that unconditionally overrides _all_ other considerations.

But, yeah, I think the baseline algorithm should be to pick the group first based on `supported_groups` and then only look at `key_share` afterwards. It's the easiest to reason about. That's what BoringSSL does, in part because I anticipated this 7 years ago. 😉 Equipreference groups is plausible, but we didn't bother with it because it wasn't really needed with the options available at the time.

To that end, if you only support a small handful of EC curves (e.g. X25519, P-256, P-384), I think one could plausibly argue that there's no real security difference and HRR avoidance is the most important factor. And indeed if OpenSSL's documented position were "we believe all named groups are truly equal preference and want to optimize for handshake round-trips", the current algorithm is just fine. But that's inconsistent with OpenSSL's docs, that say that the caller supplies a preference order. And, of course, it's also inconsistent (future) post-quantum options, very small legacy curves, or generic pluggable stuff you don't know about.

> (pqsig1,rsapsssha256),(ecdsa,eddsa)

> OpenSSL [documents](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.1/man3/SSL_set1_groups.html) that the application's supplied group list is in preference order. However, prior to 3.TBD, OpenSSL does not correctly evaluate this preference order as a TLS 1.3 server. As a result, OpenSSL server applications using post-quantum key agreements are vulnerable to a downgrade attack.

I noticed that @arapov moved this to the backlog. Given postquantum transition timelines, I'd suggest OpenSSL reconsider this. At the least, you all should include above correction to your documentation. 

Note that rfc8446bis is going to include some text clarifying that OpenSSL's behavior is incorrect. (Or rather, that OpenSSL's behavior is correct _if it believes all groups are equipreference_. That is a fine belief, but it's not what OpenSSL's documentation says. Nor is it suitable for postquantum.)

I see no incongruity with the current behaviour and the documentation. The manpage linked simply states that the functions set a preference order, not how the preferences of client and server are reconciled into an actual outcome.

Servers have always been free to determine the final choice of algorithm as they see fit. RFC 8446 does not prescribe specific behaviour here.

In general:

- An implementation strategy to minimise the initial CH size at the cost of more round-trips if both parties support a PQC KEM is valid.
- An implementation strategy to use a larger initial CH with predictive inclusion of a PQC KEM key share, leading to a larger CH but lower number of roundtrips in the server-supports-PQC case, is also valid.

These are engineering tradeoffs and there are reasons for both approaches.

As stated above, the current implementation does not really support the former case because a size-minimised initial CH will lead to a non-PQC KEM being used with a libssl server endpoint. - We should provide flexibility via some new API to allow more arbitrary policy to be implemented (via callback) for those that want to use some bespoke policy, as again a server is free to decide as it wishes.

- We should provide guidance on KEM and ciphersuite negotiation behaviours in the documentation.

What OpenSSL is doing is *NOT* client preference. The way TLS 1.3 works, the client sends a preference list in supported_groups and predicts a subset of them in key_shares for in the initial ClientHello. The specification is quite clear that the client's predicted set may be any arbitrary subset of supported_groups and need not be the most preferred groups.    completed handshake to change what groups they use in their
   "key_share" extension in subsequent connections

Related to your question regarding servers sending `supported_groups`: RFC8446 in section [4.2.7.](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446#section-4.2.7) states:
```
If the server has a group it prefers to the ones in the "key_share" extension but is still willing 
to accept the ClientHello, it SHOULD send "supported_groups" to update the client's view 
of its preferences; this extension SHOULD contain all groups the server supports, regardless

```
One can use the `SSL_CTX_set_msg_callback` in combination with `SSL_trace` to gain excellent insights of what OpenSSL does. The following snippet might help: 
```
BIO* output = BIO_new_fp(stdout, BIO_NOCLOSE); // We create a BIO for stdout

SSL_set_msg_callback(ssl, SSL_trace); // Use the built-in 'SSL_trace callback for maximum insights
```
